book_title: Chapter 3: GSSAs, Fuel Pass-Throughs & Every ₹100 of Freighter Economics
question: How does Afcom fill its planes across Asia without a retail salesforce, and what happens to ₹100 of freight revenue on its way to free cash flow?

epigraph.quote: A freighter airline can show a 40% operating margin on paper and still starve for cash if receivables stretch to ninety days while lessors demand deposits upfront.
epigraph.author: Aviation Credit Desk Note

web_blocks.html: Afcom fills its overseas freighters without opening costly foreign branch offices [5, 9]. Instead, it uses **General Sales and Service Agents (GSSAs)** across India, Hong Kong, Singapore, Thailand, Japan, South Korea, China, and Taiwan [5, 9]. GSSAs work as local sales agents on commission [5, 9]. They stay close to global freight forwarders, group cargo onto Master Air Waybills (MAWBs), clear customs papers, and collect payments [5, 9]. Afcom also uses interline deals with carriers like VietJet and Naero Air Corporation [9]. Those links carry freight beyond its own 737-800BCF routes [9].

Rules and airport access shape the supply side of air cargo. Flights depend on **bilateral Air Services Agreements (ASAs)**, DGCA safety permits, BCAS cargo screening, and airport ground slots [4, 9]. Winning **Designated Indian Carrier** status in early 2026 cut a major cost [9]. It exempted Afcom from state-level VAT on Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF) uplifted for overseas cargo flights at hubs like Chennai [9]. In FY26, jet fuel cost ~₹116.6 crore (~20% of revenue) [10]. Maintenance rentals (~₹51.9 crore), trip support (~₹44.6 crore), and residual wet-lease fees (~₹33.5 crore) made up the rest of direct costs [10].

Fuel surcharges help pass through part of ATF price swings, yet working capital tells a sharper story. Freight forwarders and GSSAs usually pay on 60-to-90-day credit terms [13, 16]. That pushed Afcom's **Debtor Days to ~85 days in FY26** (down slightly from 90–95 days in FY25), with audited trade receivables scaling from **₹59.03 crore in FY25 to ₹135.76 crore in FY26** [13, 16, 28, 30]. Meanwhile, aircraft lessors, fuel vendors, and ground handlers demand upfront deposits and fast payment [15]. That timing gap kept FY26 Operating Cash Flow (CFO) at just ₹36.00 crore against ₹122.00 crore of PAT [1, 9]. Heavy fleet deposits (-₹206.71 crore investing outflow) then drove Free Cash Flow down to -₹170.71 crore [1, 9, 15]. In H1 FY27 (ended September 30, 2026), working-capital discipline began to inflect: trade receivables stabilized at **₹134.52 crore** even as annualized revenue jumped past ₹830 crore, lifting H1 CFO to **₹49.47 crore** (55.0% of PAT) [28]. Yet trade payables simultaneously dropped from ₹28.23 crore to ₹3.24 crore and H1 investing outflows surged to **-₹214.46 crore** (lease deposits, capital advances, and subsidiary loans), leaving only **₹5.15 crore** in unrestricted operating bank accounts outside restricted QIP monitoring funds [28].

web_blocks.takeaway: For every ₹100 of FY26 revenue, Afcom generated ₹40.14 in EBITDA and ₹20.93 in PAT, but converted only ₹6.17 into CFO and -₹29.33 into FCF; H1 FY27 lifted CFO conversion to ₹11.88 per ₹100 of sales, though heavy fleet deposits kept FCF deeply negative.

web_blocks.html: Ground handling, landing fees, navigation charges, and crew positioning add quiet cost friction to every route [4, 10]. Night-cargo windows out of Chennai (MAA) and Navi Mumbai help Afcom avoid daytime passenger delays [6, 21]. Faster tarmac turns and customs clearance keep daily flight hours high on each plane [6, 21].

Heavy C-check and D-check cycles also matter for 2000-vintage Boeing 737-800BCFs [4]. Dry-lease rents on older converted planes are much lower than factory-new freighters [4]. Still, aging airframes need higher maintenance reserves and parts spending as flight hours add up [4, 10]. Investors must track those real cash outlays alongside headline EBITDA [4, 10]. Sustaining H1 FY27's receivables stabilization (₹134.52 crore on an annualized ~₹834 crore revenue base, or ~59 annualized debtor days) is equally vital [28]. Because trade payables fell sharply to ₹3.24 crore and upfront lessor deposits continue consuming equity proceeds, keeping unrestricted operating cash above the thin ₹5.15 crore September 2026 level remains a key operational watch item [28].

book_paragraphs: If you own three freighters in Chennai, how do you sell cargo space in Hong Kong, Tokyo, Taipei, and Singapore without hiring fifty overseas sales managers? Afcom solves this through General Sales and Service Agents—known in the trade as GSSAs. Think of a GSSA as an outsourced regional distributor. They sit inside major Asian cargo hubs, take bookings from multinational freight forwarders, consolidate dozens of smaller shipments onto Afcom's flights, and take a commission on every kilogram.

Pairing that GSSA network with Designated Indian Carrier status in early 2026 gave Afcom a genuine cost edge on international sectors. Aviation Turbine Fuel in India carries heavy state-level VAT, which historically punished domestic carriers. Once Afcom qualified as a Designated Indian Carrier for international cargo, it gained ATF VAT exemptions at hubs like Chennai, helping lift FY26 operating margins to 40%. Yet GSSA credit terms stretched trade receivables to ₹135.76 crore by March 2026 (up from ₹59.03 crore in FY25), before stabilizing at ₹134.52 crore in September 2026—a crucial inflection that lifted H1 FY27 operating cash flow to ₹49.47 crore even as heavy lease deposits kept unrestricted operating cash thin at ₹5.15 crore.

book_callouts.title: THE CASH-CONVERSION GAP
book_callouts.text: On paper, Afcom earned ₹20.93 of net profit on every ₹100 of FY26 sales, converting just ₹6.17 into CFO and -₹29.33 into FCF. In H1 FY27, CFO conversion improved to ₹11.88 per ₹100 of revenue (₹49.47 crore CFO on ₹416.32 crore standalone sales), yet -₹214.46 crore of H1 lease deposits and advances kept free cash flow negative at -₹164.99 crore.

book_subsections.title: Tracing ₹100 From the Tarmac to the Bank Account
paragraphs: When we trace ₹100 of Afcom's FY26 revenue through the income statement and cash-flow statement, the central tension of this business jumps right off the page. Out of every ₹100 billed, roughly ₹60 goes to direct operating costs—led by fuel, maintenance reserves, trip support, and crew—leaving ₹40.14 of operating EBITDA. After deducting ₹9.09 for depreciation (mostly on leased aircraft under Ind AS 116), ₹5.49 for interest, and ₹5.32 for taxes (offset by ₹0.86 of other income), Afcom reports ₹20.93 of net profit. By aviation standards, a 21% net margin is extraordinary.

Yet the cash-flow bridge tells a far more sobering story. Freight forwarders and GSSAs take roughly 85 days to pay their bills, while aircraft lessors and airport authorities want security deposits and maintenance reserves upfront. As a result, working capital and lease cash adjustments absorbed the bulk of accounting profits, leaving just ₹6.17 of operating cash flow per ₹100 of revenue. Layer on ₹35.51 of investing outflows for fleet expansion, and the business burned ₹29.33 of free cash flow per ₹100 of sales—explaining why Afcom had to tap institutional equity investors again in May 2026.

book_subsections.title: Fuel Pass-Throughs and the Airport Slot Bottleneck
paragraphs: Another operational detail worth understanding is how Afcom handles jet fuel volatility. In scheduled cargo, airlines levy a variable fuel surcharge linked to global ATF indices, while on-demand charters are priced on current block-hour fuel quotes. That gives Afcom partial insulation when crude spikes—provided demand stays firm enough for forwarders to accept the surcharge.

At the same time, ground handling, BCAS security screening, and night-curfew slots at congested airports like Mumbai, Bengaluru, and Singapore act as an invisible governor on daily aircraft utilization. Every hour a freighter waits for tarmac clearance is an hour it is not earning block-hour revenue.

book_subsections.title: Night-Window Turnarounds and Working-Capital Friction
paragraphs: To understand how a three-plane airline generates ₹583 crore in annual revenue, you have to watch the clock on the Chennai tarmac. Freighters make money only when their wheels are in the air, so rapid two-to-three-hour ground turnarounds during off-peak night windows are essential. By basing operations in Chennai and tapping regional hubs like Bengaluru, Delhi, and Navi Mumbai, Afcom avoids the worst daytime passenger slot congestion while connecting directly into Southeast Asian morning distribution windows.

Yet operational efficiency on the tarmac does not automatically translate into immediate cash in the bank. Freight forwarders and GSSA partners routinely settle invoices on 60-to-90-day credit terms, pushing Afcom's debtor days to 85 in FY26. Meanwhile, aircraft lessors, fuel suppliers, and airport authorities demand timely payment or upfront security deposits—creating a structural working-capital gap that management must bridge before unit economics look as clean in cash flow as they do on the income statement.

book_subsections.title: The Hidden Maintenance Math of 2000-Vintage Freighters
paragraphs: There is an old aviation saying that older airplanes are cheap to lease and expensive to keep airworthy. Afcom's first two Boeing 737-800BCFs—VT-AFO and VT-AFC—are 2000-vintage airframes converted from passenger service into freighters. Dry-leasing converted narrowbodies keeps monthly fixed lease rentals far below what a brand-new freighter would cost, which is a smart way for an emerging cargo airline to enter the market.

Yet every flight hour on a twenty-five-year-old airframe accrues heavy maintenance obligations—C-checks, landing-gear overhauls, and engine shop visits—alongside monthly lessor maintenance reserves. That is why you and I always look past headline EBITDA to see how much cash remains after maintenance capex and lease deposits.

That working-capital tension is the bridge between unit economics and financial forensics. An airline can earn 40 percent EBITDA margins on every flight hour and still consume cash if freight-forwarder receivables stretch to 85 days and aircraft lessors demand upfront deposits for each additional narrowbody added to the certificate.

Fuel tax policy is another quiet pillar of those margins. Designated Indian Carrier status exempts jet fuel uplifted on international sectors from steep state Value Added Taxes in hubs like Tamil Nadu, creating a structural cost advantage over non-scheduled ad-hoc operators.
With those unit economics clear, Chapter 4 widens the lens to compare Afcom against domestic rivals and two illuminating international and Indian historical parallels.
